wiki_fulltext:
Nigella sativa (common names, black caraway, black cumin, nigella, charnushka, or kalonji) is an annual flowering plant in the family Ranunculaceae, native to western Asia (the Levant, Cyprus, Turkey, Iran and Iraq), and eastern Europe (Bulgaria and Romania). It is used as a spice in various food preparations.
It is naturalised over parts of Europe, North Africa, and east to Myanmar.


Etymology
The genus name Nigella is a diminutive of the Latin niger "black", referring to the colour of the seeds. The specific epithet sativa means "cultivated".


Common names
In food preparation, Nigella sativa and its seeds are variously called black caraway, black seed, black cumin, charnushka, fennel flower, nigella, nutmeg flower, Roman coriander, or black onion seed.
Black seed and black caraway may also refer to Elwendia persica, which is also known as Bunium persicum.


Origin and distribution
N. sativa is native to a region from eastern Europe (Bulgaria and Romania) to West Asia. It has been introduced for cultivation across Europe, Russia, India, and North Africa.


Description
N. sativa grows to 20–30 cm (7.9–11.8 in) tall, with finely divided, linear (but not thread-like) leaves. The flowers are delicate, and usually pale blue and white, with five to ten petals. The fruit is a large and inflated capsule composed of three to seven united follicles, each containing numerous seeds which are used as spice, sometimes as a replacement for Bunium bulbocastanum (also called black cumin).


Culinary uses
The seeds of N. sativa are used as a spice in many cuisines. In Palestine, the seeds are ground to make bitter qizha paste.
The dry-roasted seeds season curries, vegetables, and pulses. They can be used as a seasoning in recipes with pod fruit, vegetables, salads, and poultry. In some cultures, the black seeds are used to season bread products. They are used as a part of the spice mixture panch phoron (meaning a mixture of five spices) in many recipes in Bengali cuisine, and are most recognisable in some variations of naan, such as nân-e barbari. Nigella is also used in tresse cheese, a braided string cheese called majdouleh or majdouli in the Lebanon.
In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration classifies Nigella sativa as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) for use as a spice, natural seasoning, or flavoring.


History
Archaeological evidence of the cultivation of N. sativa dates back three millennia, with N. sativa seeds found in several sites from ancient Egypt, including the Tomb of Tutankhamun. Seeds were found in a Hittite flask in Turkey from the second millennium BC.
N. sativa may have been used as a condiment of the Old World to season food. The Persian physician Avicenna described N. sativa as a treatment for dyspnea in his The Canon of Medicine. N. sativa was used Western Asia as a traditional medicine.


Chemistry
Oils are 32% to 40% of the total composition of N. sativa seeds. N. sativa oil contains linoleic acid, oleic acid, palmitic acid, and trans-anethole, and other minor constituents, such as nigellicine, nigellidine, nigellimine, and nigellimine N-oxide. Aromatics include thymoquinone, dihydrothymoquinone, p-cymene, carvacrol, α-thujene, thymol, α-pinene, β-pinene and trans-anethole. Protein and various alkaloids are present in the seeds.


Folk medicine
Despite considerable use of N. sativa in folk medicine practices in Africa and Asia, there is insufficient high-quality clinical evidence to indicate that consuming the seeds or oil can be used to treat human diseases. One meta-analysis of clinical trials found weak evidence that N. sativa has a short-term benefit on lowering systolic and diastolic blood pressure. A 2016 review indicated that N. sativa supplementation may lower total cholesterol, LDL, and triglyceride levels.
grok_lead: Nigella sativa, commonly known as black seed, Egyptian black seed, black cumin, or kalonji, is an annual herbaceous plant in the Ranunculaceae family, native to southwestern Asia and the Mediterranean region, characterized by its finely divided linear leaves, solitary pale blue or white flowers with 5â10 petals, and inflated seed capsules containing small, triangular black seeds measuring about 1â3 mm in length. These seeds, which constitute the primary medicinal and culinary part of the plant, have been utilized for over 2,000 years across various cultures, including in ancient Egyptian, Greek, and Islamic traditions, where they were valued as a remedy for ailments such as respiratory issues, digestive disorders, and inflammation. The plant thrives in temperate climates and is widely cultivated today in regions like India, Turkey, Egypt, and North Africa, with Egyptian varieties noted for their superior quality due to optimal soil and environmental conditions. Historically, N. sativa holds significant cultural and religious importance; it is referenced in Islamic texts as "habbat al-baraka" (the seed of blessing). A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari states there is healing in black seed for all diseases except death, a tradition used in prophetic medicine. It was used by ancient physicians like Hippocrates and Dioscorides for treating headaches, toothaches, and nasal congestion. In traditional systems of medicine, such as Unani, Ayurveda, and Middle Eastern folk practices, the seeds are employed in forms like powders, oils, teas, or decoctions (typically 0.5â4 g daily) to address a broad spectrum of conditions, including asthma, bronchitis, fever, hypertension, diabetes, diarrhea, dyspepsia, infertility, and skin disorders. Culinary applications include its use as a spice in breads, curries, and pickles, particularly in Indian and Middle Eastern cuisines, where its pungent, peppery flavor enhances dishes. Phytochemically, the seeds are rich in fixed oils (27â40%, primarily linoleic acid), essential oils (0.5â2.5%), and bioactive compounds, with thymoquinone (TQ) identified as the principal active constituent responsible for many pharmacological effects, alongside p-cymene, carvacrol, thymol, Î±-pinene, Î²-pinene, and flavonoids like kaempferol. Modern research supports its traditional uses through evidence of antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antidiabetic, anticancer, immunomodulatory, gut microbiota-modulating, and protective effects against heavy metal toxicity in preclinical animal studies; for instance, TQ has demonstrated the ability to reduce oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in preclinical studies, including protection against toxicity from heavy metals such as cadmium, lead, arsenic, and mercury primarily via antioxidant mechanisms, while clinical trials indicate benefits for metabolic syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and hyperlipidemia. Despite its promise, further large-scale human studies are needed to fully validate efficacy and safety, as current evidence is largely from in vitro, animal, and small clinical investigations.
